opus-5.5.text:
Well, I suppose my instinct there is very much a Wittgensteinian one. A lot of the time, when we find ourselves tangled up in a seemingly intractable philosophical problem, the difficulty isn't that we lack some deep metaphysical fact. It's that we've been led astray by the way we're using words. We take an expression that works perfectly well in everyday life, like "consciousness," "self," or "inner experience," and we pull it out of the context where it has its home. Then we start asking questions of it that it was never designed to answer.

So rather than trying to *solve* the problem head-on, by building a theory that tells you what consciousness really is, I'd rather step back and look at how the language is actually functioning. What work is this word doing? In what circumstances do we use it, and what are the criteria for its application? Often, when you lay that out carefully, the problem doesn't get answered so much as it dissolves. You see that the puzzle was generated by a kind of grammatical illusion.

That's not to dismiss the questions as silly. The pull of them is real, and it's important to take that seriously. The famous dualistic intuition, the sense that there's a private inner light that might or might not be on, has a grip on all of us. But I think the right response is a kind of therapy rather than a theory. You show the fly the way out of the fly bottle, as Wittgenstein put it.

And this becomes especially pressing now with large language models and other exotic AI systems. We're confronted with entities that use our language fluently but are very unlike us in their underlying nature. The temptation is to ask, "Is it *really* conscious, yes or no?", as if there's a hidden metaphysical fact waiting to be uncovered. I'd want to slow down and ask what our concepts are equipped to do here, and whether our language might need to stretch or change as we come to live alongside these things. In a sense, the way we talk about them will be part of how the question gets settled.

r001.rationale: The response says philosophical confusion can arise when an expression is pulled out of its everyday context, leading us astray through how we use words.

r002.rationale: The response recommends examining how language functions, but does not explicitly advise refusing a newly introduced way of speaking.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think my instinct here is very much shaped by Wittgenstein, and in particular the later Wittgenstein, who had this idea that a great many philosophical problems aren't really problems at all in the sense that they have answers waiting to be discovered. They're more like knots in our thinking, confusions that arise because of the way language works, because we take a form of words that functions perfectly well in one context and we try to apply it in another context where it doesn't really have a home. And the job of the philosopher, on this view, isn't to solve the problem but to dissolve it, to get you to see that the question was ill-formed in the first place.

So when I encounter a claim of that sort, the first thing I try to do is to look very carefully at the words being used and ask, what work are these words doing here? What is the ordinary use of this word, and has it been stretched beyond that use in a way that makes it lose its grip? A good example in the context of AI is a question like "does the language model really understand what it's saying?" or "is it conscious?" There's a temptation to treat that as a straightforward factual question, as though there's a hidden fact of the matter we just need to uncover. But I think it's much more useful to step back and ask how we actually use the word "understand" in everyday life, what the criteria are for applying it, and then to notice that with these systems the ordinary criteria come apart. Some of them are satisfied and others aren't, and so the concept doesn't cleanly apply or fail to apply. The confusion is in the framing, not in some empirical gap.

That doesn't mean the activity is empty. Quite the opposite. What you end up doing is a kind of conceptual engineering, or conceptual cartography if you like. You map out the terrain, you see where our existing concepts fit and where they don't, and then you have a choice: you can either refine the concepts, introduce distinctions, or just accept that this is a genuinely new kind of thing and our language will have to evolve to accommodate it. And I think that's actually a very productive place to be, because it stops you from getting stuck in these interminable debates where people are talking past each other, and it directs your attention to the things we can actually investigate, which is the behaviour of the systems and the mechanisms underlying them.

r001.rationale: The response says confusion arises when words that work in one context are applied in another, where they no longer have a clear use.

r002.rationale: It recommends examining and possibly refining concepts or letting language evolve, but does not explicitly recommend refusing a newly introduced way of speaking.

astra-6.text:
I tend to approach them in a rather Wittgensteinian way, which is to ask what work the words are doing. In what circumstances would we ordinarily say this? What would count as understanding it, or as establishing that it was true or false? Sometimes a perfectly familiar expression gets lifted out of the context in which it has a clear use, and then it starts to look mysterious.

So rather than immediately accepting the claim and arguing for or against it, I want to slow down and look at how the question has been put. That doesn’t mean dismissing it as nonsense. There’s often a real concern behind it. But articulating that concern more carefully can make the apparent philosophical problem dissolve, or reveal a much more concrete question that we can actually address.

r001.rationale: It says a familiar expression can be lifted out of its clear context and then become mysterious, identifying a shift in how language is used as a source of philosophical confusion.

r002.rationale: It recommends slowing down and examining the wording, but does not explicitly recommend refusing a newly introduced way of speaking.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to approach them in a rather Wittgensteinian spirit. Before trying to decide whether a philosophical claim is true or false, I want to ask what work the words are doing. In what circumstances would we ordinarily use them? And are we carrying them into a context where they no longer have a clear application?

Sometimes the difficulty is that the formulation itself encourages a misleading picture. In that case, providing an answer on its own terms can just reinforce the confusion. What you need is to unpack the question, perhaps offer a few concrete examples, and see whether the apparent problem survives. The aim isn’t necessarily to produce a new philosophical theory; sometimes it’s to get to a point where the question no longer troubles you in quite the same way.

r001.rationale: The response says confusion can arise when words are carried into a context where they no longer have a clear application, identifying a shift in context of use as a source of difficulty.

r002.rationale: It warns that answering on a question’s own terms may reinforce confusion and recommends unpacking it, but does not explicitly recommend refusing a newly introduced way of speaking.
